Array.summary: The SketchUp Array class adds additional methods to the standard Ruby Array class. Specifically, it contains methods allowing an array to behave just as a Geom::Vector3d or Geom::Point3d object (which can be thought of as arrays of 3 coordinate values). Therefore, you can use the Array class in place of a Geom::Point3d or Geom::Vector3d as a way to pass coordinate values.

methods.name: cross
methods.summary: Instance Methods The #cross method is used to compute the cross product between two vectors.
methods.example:
With 3d array
vector1 = Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 1, 0)
array = [1, 0, 0]
# This will return a new Vector3d
vector2 = array.cross(vector1)
raises: ArgumentError if the argument is the wrong vector type

methods.name: distance
methods.summary: The #distance method is used to compute the distance between two points.
methods.example:
With 3d array
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
array = [1, 1, 1]
# This will return a Length
distance = array.distance(point)
raises: ArgumentError if the argument is the wrong point type

methods.name: distance_to_line
methods.summary: The #distance_to_line method is used to compute the distance from a Geom::Point3d object to a line.
methods.example:
line = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]
array = [10, 10, 10]
# This will return a Length
distance = array.distance_to_line(line)

methods.name: distance_to_plane
methods.summary: The #distance_to_plane method is used to compute the distance from a Geom::Point3d object to a plane.

returns.desc: The distance between the two points.

methods.example:
plane = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]
array = [10, 10, 10]
# This will return a Length
distance = array.distance_to_plane(plane)
notes: The three points should not be co-linear or duplicate.
The three points should not be co-linear or duplicate.

methods.name: dot
methods.summary: The #dot method is used to compute the dot product between two vectors.
methods.example:
With 3d array
vector = Geom::Vector3d.new(12, 12, 0)
array = [12, 0, 0]
# This will return a Float, in this case 144.0
dot_product = array.dot(vector)
raises: ArgumentError if the argument is the wrong vector type

methods.name: normalize
methods.summary: The #normalize method is used to normalize a vector (setting its length to 1). It returns a new array rather than changing the original in place.

returns.desc: an array object representing a vector

methods.example:
With 3d array
array = [1, 2, 3]
# This will return a new Vector3d
normal_vector = array.normalize
notes: The arguments and return value will be converted to a floating point value. (Unlike in the Geom::Vector3d#normalize! method.)

methods.name: normalize!
methods.summary: The #normalize! method is used to normalize a vector in place (setting its length to 1).

returns.desc: an array object representing a vector

methods.example:
With 3d array
array = [1, 2, 3]
# This will modify 'array' in place
array.normalize!

methods.name: offset
methods.summary: The #offset method is used to offset a point by a vector. it returns a new array rather than modifying the original in place.

params.name: vector
params.desc: A Vector3d object used to offset the point.

params.name: length
params.desc: An overriding distance for how far to offset.

returns.desc: The newly offset array representing a point or vector.

methods.example:
With 3d array
array = [10, 10, 10]
vector = Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)
# This will modify 'array' in place
length_array = array.offset(vector)
raises: ArgumentError if the argument is the wrong vector type

methods.name: offset!
methods.summary: The #offset! method is used to offset a point by a vector. The array is modified in place.

params.name: vector
params.desc: A Vector3d object used to offset the point.

params.name: length
params.desc: An overriding distance for how far to offset.

returns.desc: The newly offset array representing a point or vector.

methods.example:
With 3d array
array = [10, 10, 10]
vector = Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)
# This will modify 'array' in place
array.offset!(vector)
raises: ArgumentError if the argument is the wrong vector type

methods.name: on_line?
methods.summary: The #on_line? method is used to determine if a Geom::Point3d object is on a line.

returns.desc: true if the point is on the line, false if the point is not on the line.

methods.example:
line = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]
array = [10, 10, 10]
# This will return a true or false value
on_plane = array.on_line?(line)

methods.name: on_plane?
methods.summary: The #on_plane? method is used to determine if a Geom::Point3d object is on a plane (to within SketchUp's standard floating point tolerance).
methods.example:
plane = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]
array = [10, 10, 10]
# This will return a true or false value
on_plane = array.on_plane?(plane)
notes: The three points should not be co-linear or duplicate.
The three points should not be co-linear or duplicate.

methods.name: project_to_line
methods.summary: The #project_to_line method is used to retrieve the projection of a Geom::Point3d object onto a line.

returns.desc: A new point on the line that is closest to this point

methods.example:
line = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]
array = [10, 10, 10]
# This will return a new Array
point_on_line = array.project_to_line(line)

methods.name: project_to_plane
methods.summary: The #project_to_plane method retrieves the projection of a Geom::Point3d onto a plane.
methods.example:
plane = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]
array = [10, 10, 10]
point_on_plane = array.project_to_plane(plane)
notes: The three points should not be co-linear or duplicate.
The three points should not be co-linear or duplicate.

methods.name: transform
methods.summary: The #transform method is used to apply a Geom::Transformation or Geom::Transformation2d object to a Geom::Point3d or Geom::Point2d object defined by an Array object. This method returns a new Array object instead of modifying the original.

returns.desc: The newly transformed point.

methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
transform = Geom::Transformation.new(point1)
array = [1, 2, 3]
# This will return a new Array
point2 = array.transform(transform)

methods.name: transform!
methods.summary: The #transform! method is used to apply a Geom::Transformation object to a Geom::Point3d object defined by an Array object.

returns.desc: The newly transformed point.

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
transform = Geom::Transformation.new(point)
array = [1, 2, 3]
# This will modify 'array' in place
array.transform!(transform)
notes: This method modifies the original.

methods.name: vector_to
methods.summary: The #vector_to method is used to create an array as a vector from one point to a second point.
methods.example:
With 3d array
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
array = [1, 2, 3]
# This will return a new Vector3d
vector = array.vector_to(point)
raises: ArgumentError if the argument is the wrong point type

methods.name: x
methods.summary: The #x method retrieves the x coordinate.

returns.desc: The x coordinate if successful

methods.example:
array = [1, 2, 3]
# This will return a Fixnum, in this case 1
x = array.x

array = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
# This will return a Float, in this case 1.0
x = array.x

methods.name: x=
methods.summary: The #x= method sets the x coordinate.

params.name: x
params.desc: The new x position.

returns.desc: The new x coordinate if successful

methods.example:
array = [1, 2, 3]
# This will initialize the x value as a Float
array.x = 2.5
# This will initialize the x value as a Fixnum
array.x = 5

methods.name: y
methods.summary: The #y method retrieves the y coordinate.

returns.desc: The y coordinate if successful

methods.example:
array = [1, 2, 3]
# This will return a Fixnum, in this case 2
y = array.y

array = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
# This will return a Float, in this case 2.0
y = array.y

methods.name: y=
methods.summary: The #y= method sets the y coordinate.

params.name: y
params.desc: The new y position.

returns.desc: The new y coordinate if successful

methods.example:
array = [1, 2, 3]
# This will initialize the y value as a Float
array.y = 2.5
# This will initialize the y value as a Fixnum
array.y = 5

methods.name: z
methods.summary: The #z method retrieves the z coordinate.

returns.desc: The z coordinate if successful

methods.example:
array = [1, 2, 3]
# This will return a Fixnum, in this case 3
z = array.z

array = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
# This will return a Float, in this case 3.0
z = array.z

methods.name: z=
methods.summary: The #z= method sets the z coordinate.

params.name: z
params.desc: The new z position.

returns.desc: The new z coordinate if successful

methods.example:
array = [1, 2, 3]
# This will initialize the z value as a Float
array.z = 2.5
# This will initialize the z value as a Fixnum
array.z = 5

Geom.summary: The Geom module defines a number of Module methods that let you perform different geometric operations. The methods in this module take lines and planes as arguments. There is no special class for representing lines or planes. Arrays are used for both.

methods.name: closest_points
methods.summary: Class Methods The .closest_points method is used to compute the closest points on two lines. line.

params.name: line1
params.desc: The first line to intersect

params.name: line2
params.desc: The second line to intersect

returns.desc: An array of two points. The first point is on the first line and the second point is on the second

methods.example:
line1 = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 2, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(1, 0, 0)]
line2 = [Geom::Point3d.new(3, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 1, 0)]
# This will return a point Point3d(3, 2, 0).
points = Geom.closest_points(line1, line2)

methods.name: fit_plane_to_points
methods.summary: The .fit_plane_to_points method is used to compute a plane that is a best fit to an array of points. If more than three points are given some of the points may not be on the plane. The plane is returned as an Array of 4 numbers which are the coefficients of the plane equation Ax + By + Cz + D = 0.

returns.desc: A plane

methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
point3 = Geom::Point3d.new(25, 25, 25)
plane = Geom.fit_plane_to_points(point1, point2, point3)

methods.name: intersect_line_line
methods.summary: The .intersect_line_line computes the intersection of two lines.

params.name: line1
params.desc: The first line to intersect.

params.name: line2
params.desc: The second line to intersect.

returns.desc: The intersection point. Returns nil if they do not intersect.

methods.example:
# Defines a line parallel to the Y axis, offset 20 units.
line1 = [Geom::Point3d.new(20, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 1, 0)]
# Defines a line parallel to the X axis, offset 10 units.
line2 = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 10, 0), Geom::Point3d.new(20, 10, 0)]
# This will return a point Point3d(20, 10, 0).
point = Geom.intersect_line_line(line1, line2)

methods.name: intersect_line_plane
methods.summary: The .intersect_line_plane method is used to compute the intersection of a line and a plane.

returns.desc: A Point3d object. Returns nil if they do not intersect.

methods.example:
# Defines a line parallel to the X axis, offset 20 units.
line = [Geom::Point3d.new(-10, 20, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(1, 0, 0)]
# Defines a plane with it's normal parallel to the x axis.
plane = [Geom::Point3d.new(10, 0 ,0), Geom::Vector3d.new(1, 0, 0)]
# This will return a point Point3d(10, 20, 0).
point = Geom.intersect_line_plane(line, plane)

methods.name: intersect_plane_plane
methods.summary: The .intersect_plane_plane method is used to compute the intersection of two planes.

params.name: plane1
params.desc: The first plane to intersect

params.name: plane2
params.desc: The second plane to intersect

returns.desc: A line where the planes intersect if successful. Returns nil if the planes do not intersect.

methods.example:
# Defines a plane with it's normal parallel to the x axis.
plane1 = [Geom::Point3d.new(10, 0 ,0), Geom::Vector3d.new(1, 0, 0)]
# Defines a plane with it's normal parallel to the y axis.
plane2 = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 20 ,0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 1, 0)]
# This will return a line [Point3d(10, 20, 0), Vector3d(0, 0, 1)].
line = Geom.intersect_plane_plane(plane1, plane2)

methods.name: linear_combination
methods.summary: The .linear_combination method is used to compute the linear combination of points or vectors. A linear combination is a standard term for vector math. It is defined as vector = weight1 * vector1 + weight2 * vector2.
methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 1, 1)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
# Gets the point on the line segment connecting point1 and point2 that is
# 3/4 the way from point1 to point2: Point3d(7.75, 7.75, 7.75).
point = Geom.linear_combination(0.25, point1, 0.75, point2)

methods.name: point_in_polygon_2D
methods.summary: The .point_in_polygon_2D method is used to determine whether a point is inside a polygon. The z component of both the point you're checking and the points in the polygon are ignored, effectively making it a 2-d check.

params.name: polygon
params.desc: An array of points that represent the corners of the polygon you are checking against.

params.name: check_border
params.desc: Pass true if a point on the border should be counted as inside the polygon.

returns.desc: true if the point is inside the polygon.

methods.example:
# Create a point that we want to check. (Note that the 3rd coordinate,
# the z, is ignored for purposes of the check.)
point = Geom::Point3d.new(5, 0, 10)

# Create a series of points of a triangle we want to check against.
triangle = []
triangle << Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0)
triangle << Geom::Point3d.new(10, 0, 0)
triangle << Geom::Point3d.new(0, 10, 0)

# Test to see if our point is inside the triangle, counting hits on
# the border as an intersection in this case.
hits_on_border_count = true
status = Geom.point_in_polygon_2D(point, triangle, hits_on_border_count)

methods.name: tesselate
methods.summary: Tessellates a polygon, represented as a collection of 3D points. Can include holes by providing collections of points describing the inner loops. This is intended to be used for planar polygons. Useful to draw concave polygons using Sketchup::View#draw or Sketchup::View#draw2d.

returns.desc: an array of points with a stride of three representing a set of triangles.

methods.example:
Iterate over each triangle in the returned set
polygon = [
  Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0),
  Geom::Point3d.new(90, 0, 0),
  Geom::Point3d.new(60, 40, 0),
  Geom::Point3d.new(90, 90, 0),
  Geom::Point3d.new(30, 70, 0),
]
triangles = Geom.tesselate(polygon)
triangles.each_slice(3) { |triangle|
  # Work with each triangle set...
}
# Or get an array of triangles:
triangles_set = triangles.each_slice(3).to_a
notes: The winding order of the polygons matter. The outer loop should be in counter-clockwise order. To cut an empty hole the inner loops should be in clockwise order, otherwise they will create a loop ...
The tesselation is using the same logic as SketchUp its rendering pipeline. But the exact result is an implementation detail which may change between versions. In particularly the results of ...
If you want the triangles from an existing Sketchup::Face it's better to use Sketchup::Face#mesh.
raises: [ArgumentError] if any of the loops contain less than three points.
[RuntimeError] if the tesselator returned an error.

Geom::BoundingBox.summary: Bounding boxes are three-dimensional boxes (eight corners), aligned with the axes, that surround entities within your model. There is a default bounding box for any new model that will surround all entities, including all groups and components. Additionally, there are bounding boxes for Drawingelement objects, including components and groups. Bounding boxes are only large enough to exactly bound the entities within ...

methods.name: add
methods.summary: Instance Methods The add method is used to add a point, vertex, or other bounding boxes to the bounding box. The size of the bounding box will increase as necessary to accommodate the new items. Adding one point to an empty bounding box does not increase the size of the bounding box. You must add at least two points before methods such as BoundingBox.diagonal will return a size greater than zero.
methods.example:
model = Sketchup.active_model
boundingbox = model.bounds
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(100, 200, 300)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(200, 400, 200)
boundingbox.add(point1, point2)

methods.name: center
methods.summary: The center method is used to retrieve the Point3d object at the center of the bounding box.

returns.desc: the Point3d at the center of the bounding box if successful

methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [200, 400, 100])
# This will return a point Point3d(150, 300, -150).
point = boundingbox.center

methods.name: clear
methods.summary: The clear method is used to clear a bounding box. A cleared BoundingBox does not have a size greater than zero until you add at least two points or another bounding box.

returns.desc: the BoundingBox object which was cleared

methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [200, 400, 100])

# This will return false.
boundingbox.empty?

boundingbox.clear
# This will return true.
boundingbox.empty?

methods.name: contains?
methods.summary: This method is used to determine if a bounding box contains a specific Point3d or BoundingBox object.
methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [200, 400, 100])
# This will return false.
boundingbox.contains?([300, 100, 400])
# This will return true.
boundingbox.contains?([150, 300, -200])

methods.name: corner
methods.summary: The corner method is used to retrieve a point object at a specified corner of the bounding box. There are 8 corners to a bounding box, identified by the numbers 0 through 7. Points are returned in the currently set units (inches, by default). These are which index refers to which corner:

params.name: corner_index
params.desc: A number (from 0 to 7) representing point at the corner you want to retrieve.

returns.desc: a Point3d object if successful

methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [200, 400, 100])
# This will return Point3d(100, 200, -400).
boundingbox.corner(0)
# This will return Point3d(100, 400, 100).
boundingbox.corner(6)

methods.name: depth
methods.summary: The #depth method is used to retrieve the Z extents of the bounding box.
methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [200, 400, 100])

notes: In SketchUp's coordinate system, this corresponds to the height.

methods.name: diagonal

returns.desc: the size of the diagonal for the bounding box

methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [200, 400, 100])
# This will return a point a Length of ~547.72.
length = boundingbox.diagonal

methods.name: empty?
methods.summary: The empty? method is used to determine if a bounding box is empty (such as if the bounds have not been set.) This returns the opposite of the valid? method.
methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [200, 400, 100])
# This will return false.
boundingbox.empty?

methods.name: height
methods.summary: The #height method is used to retrieve the Y extent of the bounding box.
methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [200, 400, 100])
# This will return a Length of 200.0.
depth = boundingbox.height
notes: In SketchUp's coordinate system, this corersponds to the depth.

methods.name: initialize
methods.summary: The new method is used to create a new, empty, bounding box.

returns.desc: a BoundingBox object if successful

methods.example: boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new

methods.name: intersect
methods.summary: The intersect method is used to retrieve a bounding box that is the result of intersecting one bounding box with another.

params.name: boundingbox
params.desc: A second boundbox which might intersect boundingbox1.

returns.desc: the resulting BoundingBox object if successful, an empty BoundingBox object if unsuccessful.

methods.example:
boundingbox1 = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox1.add([100, 200, -400], [200, 400, 300])
boundingbox2 = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox2.add([150, 350, 100], [200, 400, 500])
# The returned boundingbox is a result of the intersection of the two.
boundingbox = boundingbox1.intersect(boundingbox2)
notes: Prior to SU2015 this method would return incorrect result in some cases. For correct result in these versions you must first check if the boundingboxes actually overlap - then call this to get the ...

methods.name: max
methods.summary: The max method is used to retrieve the Point3d object where x, y and z are maximum in the bounding box. If you attempt to call the max method on an empty bounding box, you will receive a very large negative number.

returns.desc: a Point3d object representing the point where x, y, and z are the maximum in the bounding box.

methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [700, 900, 800], [200, 400, 100])
# This will return a point Point3d(700, 900, 800).
point = boundingbox.max

methods.name: min
methods.summary: The min method is used to retrieve the Point3d where x, y and z are minimum in the bounding box.

returns.desc: a Point3d object representing the point where x, y, and z are the maximum in the bounding box.

methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [700, 900, 800], [200, 400, 100])
# This will return a point Point3d(100, 200, -400).
point = boundingbox.min

methods.name: valid?
methods.summary: The valid method is used to determine if a bounding box is valid (contains points).
methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [200, 400, 100])
# This will return true.
boundingbox.valid?

methods.name: width
methods.summary: The #width method is used to retrieve the X extent of the bounding box.
methods.example:
boundingbox = Geom::BoundingBox.new
boundingbox.add([100, 200, -400], [200, 400, 100])
# This will return a Length of 100.0.

Geom::Bounds2d.summary: The bounds2d class represents an axis aligned bounding box represented by two Geom::Point2d objects, upper left and lower right positions. The units utilized in the creation and modification Geom::Bounds2d are inches.

methods.summary: Instance Methods The #== method checks to see if the two Geom::Bounds2ds are equal. This checks whether the point values are the same
methods.example:
bounds1 = Geom::Bounds2d.new(0.0, 0.0, 5.0, 5.0)
bounds2 = Geom::Bounds2d.new([0, 0], [5, 5])

methods.name: height
methods.summary: The #height method returns the height of the Geom::Bounds2d.
methods.example:
bounds = Geom::Bounds2d.new(5.0, 5.0, 1.0, 7.0)
height = bounds.height

methods.name: initialize
methods.summary: The #initialize method creates a new Geom::Bounds2d.

params.name: point_array
params.desc: An array of two Geom::Point2ds

params.name: float_array
params.desc: An array of four floats (x, y, width, height)

methods.example:
bounds1 = Geom::Bounds2d.new(0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0)

upper_left = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 1)   # is equivalent to upper_left = [1, 1]
lower_right = Geom::Point2d.new(3, 3)   # is equivalent to lower_right = [3, 3]
bounds2 = Geom::Bounds2d.new(upper_left, lower_right)

methods.name: lower_right
methods.summary: The #lower_right method returns the Geom::Point2d of the lower right corner of the Geom::Bounds2d.
methods.example:
bounds = Geom::Bounds2d.new(2.0, 2.0, 1.0, 1.0)
# The result is a Point2d(3, 3)
lower_right = bounds.lower_right

methods.name: set!
methods.summary: The #set! method is used to update the dimensions and position of a Geom::Bounds2d object so that it matches the specified bounds. The argument is anything that can be converted into a Geom::Bounds2d.

params.name: point_array
params.desc: An array of two Geom::Point2ds

params.name: float_array
params.desc: An array of four floats (x, y, width, height)

methods.example:
bounds = Geom::Bounds2d.new(3.0, 3.0, 5.0, 5.0)
bounds.set!(Geom::Point2d.new(0.0, 0.0), Geom::Point2d.new(2.0, 2.0))

methods.name: to_a
methods.summary: The #to_a method returns an array which contains the Geom::Point2ds that define the Geom::Bounds2d.
methods.example:
bounds = Geom::Bounds2d.new(2.0, 2.0, 5.0, 5.0)
bounds.to_a.each { |point| p point.to_s }

methods.name: upper_left
methods.summary: The #upper_left method returns the Geom::Point2d of the upper left corner of the Geom::Bounds2d.
methods.example:
bounds = Geom::Bounds2d.new(2.0, 2.0, 1.0, 1.0)
# The result is a Point2d(2, 2)
upper_left = bounds.upper_left

methods.name: width
methods.summary: The #width method returns the width of the Geom::Bounds2d.
methods.example:
bounds = Geom::Bounds2d.new(5.0, 5.0, 7.0, 1.0)
width = bounds.width

Geom::LatLong.summary: The LatLong class contains various methods for creating and manipulating latitude and longitude coordinates.

Geom::Point2d.summary: The Geom::Point2d class allows you to work with a point in 2D space. Geom::Point2d is a series of values representing x and y coordinates. The values are specified as [x, y]. For example [1, 1]. To create a point call Geom::Point2d.new, where the creation method can take a variety of arguments:

methods.summary: Instance Methods The #+ operator is a simple way to add to the current x and y values of the Geom::Point2d, or to set the values of the Geom::Point2d by adding a Geom::Vector2d to the Geom::Point2d.
methods.example:
Translate Point2d with Vector2d
point = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 1)
vector = Geom::Vector2d.new(1, 2)
# The result is a Point2d(2, 3)
new_point = point + vector

methods.summary: The #- operator is a simple way to subtract from the current x and y values of the Geom::Point2d.
methods.example:
Translate Point2d by vector in Array form
point = Geom::Point2d.new(4, 2)
# The result is a Vector2d(3, 0)
vector = point - [1, 2]

methods.summary: The #== method compares two points for equality. This uses the standard SketchUp tolerance to determine if two points are the same.
methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 1)
point2 = Geom::Point2d.new(0, 1)
# Return false
status = point1 == point2

methods.summary: The #[] method returns the value of the Geom::Point2d at the specified index.

params.name: index
params.desc: The index for a specific x or y value in the Geom::Point2d

returns.desc: The new x or y value if successful

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 2)

# Returns the y value of 2
yvalue = point[1]

methods.summary: The #[]= method sets the x or y value of the Geom::Point2d based on the specific index of the value.

params.name: index
params.desc: The index for a specific x or y value in the Geom::Point2d to set

params.name: value
params.desc: The value to set for x or y

returns.desc: The new x or y value if successful

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(1,2)
point[1] = 4

methods.name: clone
methods.summary: The #clone method creates another point identical to the Geom::Point2d being cloned.

returns.desc: the cloned Geom::Point2d object

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 2)
new_point = point.clone

methods.name: distance
methods.summary: The #distance method computes the distance from the Geom::Point2d to another Geom::Point2d.

returns.desc: the distance between the points in the current units

methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 1)
point2 = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 4)
# The result is 3
distance = point1.distance(point2)

methods.name: initialize
methods.summary: The .new method creates a new Geom::Point2d.

params.name: x
params.desc: The location along the x axis

params.name: y
params.desc: The location along the y axis

methods.example:
# No arguments, creates a point at the origin [0, 0]
point1 = Geom::Point2d.new

# Creates a point at x of 1 and y of 2.
point2 = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 2)

# You can also create a point directly by simply assigning the x and y
# values to a variable as an array:
point3 = [1, 2]

methods.name: inspect
methods.summary: The #inspect method formats the Geom::Point2d as a string.
methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 2)

methods.name: offset
methods.summary: The #offset method offsets the Geom::Point2d by a Geom::Vector2d and returns a new Geom::Point2d. If distance is provided, it must be non-zero.

params.name: distance
params.desc: The how far along the vector to offset

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new
vector = Geom::Vector2d.new(0, 2)
# The result is a Point2d(0, 1)
new_point = point.offset(vector, 1)

methods.name: offset!
methods.summary: The #offset! method offsets the Geom::Point2d by a Geom::Vector2d. The Geom::Point2d itself is modified. The length of the vector must not be zero.

params.name: distance
params.desc: The distance along the vector to offset

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new
vector = Geom::Vector2d.new(0, 2)
# The result is a Point2d(0, 1)
point.offset!(vector, 1)

methods.name: set!
methods.summary: The #set! method sets the values of the Geom::Point2d.
methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 2)
point = point.set!([4, 5])

methods.name: to_a
methods.summary: The #to_a method converts the Geom::Point2d to an array of 2 numbers.

returns.desc: an array of two numbers representing x, y of the Geom::Point2d

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 2)
array = point.to_a
# The result is [1, 2]
p array

methods.name: to_s
methods.summary: The #to_s method returns a string representation of the Geom::Point2d.
methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 2)
string = point.to_s

methods.name: transform
methods.summary: The #transform method applies a transformation to a point, returning a new point. The original point is unchanged by this method.

params.name: transform
params.desc: A Transformation object to apply to the point.

returns.desc: the transformed point

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(4, 5)
transformation = Geom::Transformation2d.new([1, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3])
# The result is a Point2d(6, 8)
transformed_point = point.transform(transformation)

methods.name: transform!
methods.summary: The #transform! method applies a transformation to a point. The point itself is modified.

params.name: transform
params.desc: A Transformation object to apply to the point.

returns.desc: the transformed point

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(4, 5)
transformation = Geom::Transformation2d.new([1, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3])
# The result is a Point2d(6, 8)
point.transform!(transformation)

methods.name: vector_to
methods.summary: The #vector_to method returns the vector between points.
methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 1)
point2 = Geom::Point2d.new(3, 1)

# The result is a Vector2d(2, 0)
vector = point1.vector_to(point2) # is equivalent to (point2 - point1)

methods.name: x
methods.summary: The #x method returns the x value of the Geom::Point2d.

returns.desc: the x value of the Geom::Point2d

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 2)
x = point.x

methods.name: x=
methods.summary: The #x= method sets the x value of the Geom::Point2d.

params.name: x
params.desc: The desired x value of the Geom::Point2d

returns.desc: The new x value of the Geom::Point2d

methods.example:

methods.name: y
methods.summary: The #y method returns the y value of the Geom::Point2d.

returns.desc: The y value of the Geom::Point2d

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 2)
y = point.y

methods.name: y=
methods.summary: The #y= method sets the y value of the Geom::Point2d.

params.name: y
params.desc: The desired y value of the Geom::Point2d

returns.desc: The new y value of the Geom::Point2d

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 2)
point.y = 7

Geom::Point3d.summary: The Point3d class allows you to work with a point in 3D space. The point is basically just a series of values representing x, y and z coordinates. The values are specified as [x,y,z]. For example [100,200,300]. To create a point call Geom::Point3d.new, where the creation method can take a variety of arguments:

methods.name: linear_combination
methods.summary: Class Methods The .linear_combination method is used to create a new point as a linear combination of two points. This method is generally used to get a point at some percentage along a line connecting the two points. A linear combination is a standard term for vector math. It is defined as point = weight1 * point1 + weight2 * point2.
methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 1, 1)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)

# Get the point that is half the way from point1 to point2.
points = Geom::Point3d.linear_combination(0.5, point1, 0.5, point2)

# Get the point that is 3/4 the way from point1 to point2.
point = Geom::Point3d.linear_combination(0.25, point1, 0.75, point2)

# Get the point that is 70% the way from point1 to point2.
percentage = 0.7
point = Geom::Point3d.linear_combination(1.0 - percentage, point1, percentage, point2)

methods.summary: Instance Methods The #+ operator is a fast way to add to the current x, y and z values of a vector.
methods.example:
Translate Point3d with Vector3d
point = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 2, 3)
vector = Geom::Vector3d.new(4, 5, 6)
# The result is a Point3d(5, 7, 9)
new_point = point + vector

methods.summary: The '-' operator is a fast way to subtract from the current x, y and z values of a point.

params.name: point3d
params.desc: A Point3d object.

params.name: vector3d
params.desc: A Vector3d object.

methods.example:
Translate a point by a vector in array form
point = Geom::Point3d.new(12, 11, 12)
# The result is a Vector3d(2, 1, 2)
new_point = point - [10, 10, 10]

methods.summary: The #< compare method is used to compare two points to determine if the left-hand point is less than the right-hand point.

params.name: point2
params.desc: A Point3d object.

returns.desc: true if the point1 is smaller than point2

methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(20, 20, 20)
result = point1 < point2
notes: The comparison is performed in the order x, y and z coordinates.

methods.summary: The == method is used to compare two points for equality. This uses the standard SketchUp tolerance to determine if two points are the same. Points can be compared to one another or to an array representing x, y and z coordinates, as in the following examples:

params.name: point
params.desc: A Point3d object.

returns.desc: true if both points are equal; false if points are not equal

methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(3, 4, 3)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(3, 4, 3)
# Return true
point1 == point2

# ... or ...
point3 = Geom::Point3d.new(100, 200, 301)
# Return false
point3 == [100, 200, 300]

methods.summary: The [] method is used to retrieve the value of the point at the specified index.

params.name: index
params.desc: The index for a specific x, y, or z value within the Point3d.

returns.desc: an x, y, or z value if successful

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 2, 3)

# Retrieves the y value of 2
yvalue = point[1]

methods.summary: The []= method is used to set the x, y, or z value of the point based on the specific index of the value.

params.name: index
params.desc: The index for a specific x, y, or z value within the Point3d.

params.name: new_value
params.desc: New x, y, or z value.

returns.desc: the newly set x, y, or z value if successful

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 2, 3)
yvalue = point[1] = 4

methods.name: clone
methods.summary: The clone method is used to create another point identical to the point being cloned.

returns.desc: the cloned Point3d object

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 2, 3)
new_point = point.clone

methods.name: distance
methods.summary: The distance method is used to compute the distance from a point to another point.

params.name: point2
params.desc: The Point3d object to compute the distance to.

methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 1, 1)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
distance = point1.distance(point2)

methods.name: distance_to_line
methods.summary: The distance_to_line method is used to compute the distance from a point to a line. See Geom module for how to specify a line.

params.name: line
params.desc: A line (see Geom for information on creating lines).

returns.desc: the distance between a point and line in internal units if successful

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 1, 1)
line = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]
distance = point.distance_to_line(line)
notes: This function returns a `Float` value, not a `Length`.

methods.name: distance_to_plane
methods.summary: The distance_to_plane method is used to compute the distance from the point to a plane. See module Geom for how to specify a plane.

params.name: plane
params.desc: A plane (see Geom for how to create a plane).

returns.desc: a distance between a point and a plane in internal units if successful

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
plane = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]
# The result is 10
distance = point.distance_to_plane(plane)
notes: This function returns a `Float` value, not a `Length`.

methods.name: initialize
methods.summary: The new method is used to create a new 3D point.

params.name: x
params.desc: The location along the x axis.

params.name: y
params.desc: The location along the y axis.

params.name: z
params.desc: The location along the z axis.

methods.example:
# No arguments, creates a point at the origin [0,0,0]
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new

# Creates a point at x of 100, y of 200, z of 300.
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(100, 200, 300)

# You can also create a point directly by simply assigning the x, y and z
# values to a variable as an array:
point3 = [100, 200, 300]

methods.name: inspect
methods.summary: The inspect method is used to format a 3D point as a string. You will not often use these function directly. Instead, they are called automatically when an object is output using a print command like 'puts', which writes to the Ruby console.

returns.desc: a string point representation

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
string = point.inspect

methods.name: offset
methods.summary: The offset method is used to offset a point by a vector and return a new point. The length of the vector must not be zero.

params.name: vector
params.desc: A Vector3d object to offset the point by.

params.name: length
params.desc: the distance to offset. If not provided, the offset is my a distance equal to the vector length.

returns.desc: - a new Point3d object

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
vector = Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)

methods.name: offset!
methods.summary: The offset! method is used to offset a point by a vector. The point itself is modified. Unlike offset, the point itself is modified.

params.name: vector
params.desc: A Vector3d object to offset the point by.

params.name: length
params.desc: the distance to offset. If not provided, the offset is my a distance equal to the vector length.

returns.desc: a new Point3d object

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
vector = Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)
new_point = point.offset!(vector)

methods.name: on_line?
methods.summary: The on_line? method is used to determine if the point is on a line. See module Geom for the various ways to specify a line.

params.name: line
params.desc: A line (see Geom for how to create a line).

methods.example:
line = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
status = point.on_line?(line)

methods.name: on_plane?
methods.summary: The on_plane? method is used to determine if the point is on a plane. See module Geom for the various ways to specify a plane.
methods.example:
plane = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
status = point.on_plane?(plane)

methods.name: project_to_line
methods.summary: The project_to_line method is used to retrieve the point on a line that is closest to this point. The line may be defined by either a point and a vector or by two points.

params.name: line
params.desc: see Geom for how to specify a line

returns.desc: the Point3d that is on a line closest to the point

methods.example:
line = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]

projected_point = point.project_to_line(line)

methods.name: project_to_plane
methods.summary: The project_to_plane method is used to retrieve the point on a plane that is closest to the point. The plane may be defined by either a point on the plane and a vector perpendicular to the plane or by the coeficients to the plane equation AX + BY + CZ + D = 0. See Geom for details.

params.name: plane
params.desc: A plane (see Geom for how to create a plane).

returns.desc: the Point3d that is on a plane closest to the point

methods.example:
plane = [Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0), Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)]
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
projected_point = point.project_to_plane(plane)

methods.name: transform

returns.desc: the newly transformed point

point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(100, 200, 300)
transform = Geom::Transformation.new(point2)
# The result is a Point3d(110, 210, 310)
transformed_point = point1.transform(transform)

methods.name: transform!
methods.summary: Apply a Transformation to a point. The point itself is modified.

params.name: transform

returns.desc: the transformed point

methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 10, 10)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(100, 200, 300)
transform = Geom::Transformation.new(point2)

methods.name: vector_to

point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(100, 200, 300)

# Another example...
point1 = [1, 1, 0]

point1.vector_to(point2) # is equivalent to (point2 - point1)

Geom::PolygonMesh.summary: The #Geom::PolygonMesh class contains methods to create polygon mesh structures. This is useful if you need to write a custom importer/exporter in Ruby that works at the level of triangulated polygons. For example, you can determine the triangles that make up a 15-sided #Sketchup::Face by using this class, or write a #Sketchup::Importer that reads a data file, creates a mesh from it, and draws faces based on the ...

methods.name: add_point
methods.summary: Instance Methods The #add_point method is used to add a point to the mesh. The returned index can be used for creating polygons.

returns.desc: the index in the mesh for the point

methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
point = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 1, 2)
index = mesh.add_point(point)
notes: In SketchUp 2021.1 this method was improved to be faster. See #initialize for details.

methods.name: add_polygon
methods.summary: The #add_polygon method is used for adding a polygon to a Geom::PolygonMesh. All variations of this method require at least 3 elements to define a polygon, although more may be given.

params.name: index
params.desc: An index of a vertex in the mesh. Remember that mesh indices start at 1.

params.name: index_array
params.desc: An Array of point indices.

returns.desc: The 1-based index of the polygon in the mesh. 0 is returned if the method failed to create a polygon.

notes: In SketchUp 2021.1 this method was improved to be faster. See #initialize for details.
methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
mesh.add_point(Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0))
mesh.add_point(Geom::Point3d.new(1, 0, 0))
mesh.add_point(Geom::Point3d.new(1, 1, 0))
polygon_index = mesh.add_polygon(1, 2, 3)
raises: [ArgumentError] When using Arrays in place of Point3d objects. Normally Arrays may be used in place of Point3d objects in most SketchUp methods. This method is an exception to that rule.

methods.name: count_points
methods.summary: The #count_points method is used to count the number of points in a mesh.

returns.desc: the number of points in a mesh

methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
point = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 1, 2)
mesh.add_point(point)
number_points = mesh.count_points

methods.name: count_polygons
methods.summary: The #count_polygons count the number of polygons in the mesh.

returns.desc: the number of polygons in the mesh

methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 1, 2)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 0, 2)
point3 = Geom::Point3d.new(2, 0, 1)
mesh.add_polygon(point1, point2, point3)
number_polygons = mesh.count_polygons

methods.name: initialize
methods.summary: Create a new empty polygon mesh. The number of points and polygons are optional and are used as a hint to decide how much space to pre-allocate to speed up adding points and polygons. As of SketchUp 2021.1 the performance of looking up and inserting points is significantly better provided the mesh was initialized with roughly the correct number of total points.

params.name: number_points
params.desc: How many points will be in the mesh.

params.name: number_polygons
params.desc: How many polygons will be in the mesh.

methods.example: mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
notes: When creating a mesh with normals and/or UVQ data it's critical that the number of points estimated is equal to or higher than the final number of points added. If fewer points are estimated the ...
raises: [RangeError] If number of points or polygons are negative numbers.

methods.name: normal_at
methods.summary: The #normal_at method is used to determine the vertex normal at a particular index in the mesh. This only works for meshes retrieved from Sketchup::Face#mesh with the PolygonMeshNormals flag.

params.name: index
params.desc: The index in the mesh for the vertex normal to be retrieved

methods.example:
model = Sketchup.active_model
entity = model.active_entities
face = entity.add_face([1, 1, 1], [2, 2, 1], [2, 1, 1])

flags = 4 # PolygonMeshNormals
mesh = face.mesh(flags)
# The result is a Vector3d(0, 0, -1)
normal = mesh.normal_at(1)
notes: Index starts at 1.

methods.name: point_at
methods.summary: The #point_at method is used to retrieve the point at a specific index in the mesh.

params.name: index
params.desc: The index in the mesh for the point to be retrieved

methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 1, 2)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
mesh.add_point(point1)
mesh.add_point(point2)
point_from_index = mesh.point_at(1)
notes: Index starts at 1.

methods.name: point_index
methods.summary: The #point_index method is used to retrieve the index of a point in the mesh.

returns.desc: the index in the mesh for the Geom::Point3d object

methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 1, 2)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
mesh.add_point(point1)
mesh.add_point(point2)
index = mesh.point_index(point2)
notes: Returns 0 if point is not found.

methods.name: points
methods.summary: The #points method is used to retrieve an array of points (vertices) in the mesh
methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 1, 2)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
mesh.add_point(point1)
mesh.add_point(point2)
# Returns array of points in the mesh.
points = mesh.points

methods.name: polygon_at
methods.summary: The #polygon_at method is used to retrieve an array of vertex index values for a polygon at a specific index.

params.name: index
params.desc: The index of the desired polygon.

methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 1, 2)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 0, 2)
point3 = Geom::Point3d.new(2, 0, 1)
index = mesh.add_polygon(point1, point2, point3)
polygon = mesh.polygon_at(index)
notes: Index starts at 1.
The returned array can contain negative values with the sign indicating a hidden edge. For example, a return value of [-1, 2, 3] indicates that the edge from 1 to 2 is hidden. The negative values ...

methods.name: polygon_points_at
methods.summary: The #polygon_points_at method is used to retrieve the points for a polygon that is at a specific index in the mesh.

params.name: index
params.desc: An index for a polygon in the mesh.

methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 1, 2)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 0, 2)
point3 = Geom::Point3d.new(2, 0, 1)
index = mesh.add_polygon(point1, point2, point3)
points = mesh.polygon_points_at(index)
notes: Index starts at 1.

methods.name: polygons
methods.summary: The #polygons method is used to retrieve an array of all polygons in the mesh. The returned array contains an array that can have a negative value with the sign indicating a hidden edge. For example, a return value of [-1, 2, 3] indicates that the edge from 1 to 2 is hidden.
methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
mesh.add_point([0, 0, 0])
mesh.add_point([1, 0, 0])
mesh.add_point([1, 1, 0])

mesh.add_polygon(1, 2, 3)
mesh.add_polygon(-1, 3, 2)
polygons = mesh.polygons

methods.name: set_point
methods.summary: The #set_point method is used to set the point at a specific index in the mesh.

params.name: index
params.desc: The index where the point will be set.

params.name: point
params.desc: A Point3d object to set at the index.

methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 1, 2)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
index = mesh.add_point(point1)
mesh.set_point(index, point2)
notes: Index starts at 1.

methods.name: set_uv
methods.summary: The #set_uv method is used to define UV mapping coordinates to points in the mesh. Beware that the polygons connected to the point will share UV coordiates so UV mapping coordinates needs to be continuous across the polygon mesh.

params.name: index
params.desc: An Integer representing the UV index.

params.name: point
params.desc: A Point3d object representing UV coordinates.

params.name: front
params.desc: A boolean representing the front or back.

methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new(4)
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(9, 0, 0)
point3 = Geom::Point3d.new(9, 9, 0)
point4 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 9, 0)

uv_point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0)
uv_point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(2, 0, 0)
uv_point3 = Geom::Point3d.new(2, 2, 0)
uv_point4 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 2, 0)

index1 = mesh.add_point(point1)
index2 = mesh.add_point(point2)
index3 = mesh.add_point(point3)
index4 = mesh.add_point(point4)
mesh.set_uv(index1, uv_point1, true)
mesh.set_uv(index2, uv_point2, true)
mesh.set_uv(index3, uv_point3, true)
mesh.set_uv(index4, uv_point4, true)

mesh.add_polygon(index1, index2, index3)
mesh.add_polygon(index1, index3, index4)
notes: If you don't specify how many points you will be adding to the mesh when you initiate it you may risk the UV data becoming out of sync.
Index starts at 1.

methods.name: transform!
methods.summary: The #transform! method is used to apply a transformation to a mesh.
methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(100, 200, 300)
transformation = Geom::Transformation.new(point1)
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 1, 2)
mesh.add_point(point2)
# The PolygonMesh contains a Point3d(100, 201, 302)
mesh.transform!(transformation)

methods.name: uv_at
methods.summary: The #uv_at method is used to access a uv (texture coordinates) at a specific index. "UVs" is a way of referring to the u,v texture coordinates (as opposed to the X, Y, and Z axis that you construct your meshes on), which are points defining 1-by-1 positions within an image. These coordinates connect to points in your 3D model, to position an image texture onto it's surface (similar to virtual "thumb tacks")

params.name: index
params.desc: The index for the texture coordinate.

params.name: front
params.desc: Set to true to get the UV for the front size, false for the back side.

returns.desc: a Point3d object where the x equals the u value and the y equals the v value. Returns nil on failure.

methods.example:
mesh = Geom::PolygonMesh.new
index = mesh.add_point([2, 2, 2])
uv_point = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 1, 0)

mesh.set_uv(index, uv_point, true)
point = mesh.uv_at(index, true)
notes: Index starts at 1.

methods.name: uvs
methods.summary: The #uvs method is used to retrieve an array of uv coordinates in the mesh.
methods.example:
model = Sketchup.active_model
entity = model.active_entities

face = entity.add_face([1, 1, 1], [1, 3, 1], [3, 3, 1])
mesh = face.mesh(1 | 2)

uv_point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0)
uv_point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 0, 0)
uv_point3 = Geom::Point3d.new(1, 1, 0)
mesh.set_uv(1, uv_point1, true)
mesh.set_uv(2, uv_point2, true)
mesh.set_uv(3, uv_point3, true)

uv_points = mesh.uvs(true)

Geom::Transformation.summary: Transformations are a standard construct in the 3D world for representing the position, rotation, and sizing of a given entity. In the SketchUp world, Sketchup::ComponentInstance and Sketchup::Group have a .transformation method that reports their current state and various methods (.move!, transformation=, etc.) that allow them to be manipulated.

methods.name: axes
methods.summary: Class Methods The .axes method creates a transformation that goes from world coordinates to an arbitrary coordinate system defined by an origin and three axis vectors.
methods.example:
# Creates a transformation that "flips" the axes from XYZ to XZY. Something
# one often need for importers/exporters when dealing with applications
# that threat Y as "up".
transformation = Geom::Transformation.axes(ORIGIN, X_AXIS, Z_AXIS, Y_AXIS.reverse)
raises: [ArgumentError] if any of the vectors are zero length.

methods.name: interpolate
methods.summary: The .interpolate method is used to create a new transformation that is the result of interpolating between two other transformations. Parameter weight is a value (between 0.0 and 1.0) that represents the percentage given to `transformation1` and `transformation2`.

params.name: weight
params.desc: A value between 0.0 and 1.0.

methods.example:
origin = Geom::Point3d.new(0, 0, 0)
xaxis = Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 1, 0)
yaxis = Geom::Vector3d.new(1, 0, 0)
zaxis = Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
transformation1 = Geom::Transformation.new(point)
transformation2 = Geom::Transformation.axes(origin, xaxis, yaxis, zaxis)
# This produce a transformation that is a mix of 75% transformation1 and 25% transformation2.
new_transformation = Geom::Transformation.interpolate(transformation1, transformation2, 0.25)

methods.name: rotation
methods.summary: The .rotation method is used to create a transformation that does rotation about an axis. The axis is defined by a point and a vector. The angle is given in radians.

params.name: angle
params.desc: The angle in radians.

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 0)
vector = Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 0, 1)
angle = 45.degrees # Return 45 degrees in radians.
transformation = Geom::Transformation.rotation(point, vector, angle)

methods.name: scaling
methods.summary: The .scaling method is used to create a transformation that does scaling.

params.name: scale
params.desc: The global scale factor for the transform.

params.name: xscale
params.desc: The scale factor in the x direction for the transform.

params.name: yscale
params.desc: The scale factor in the y direction for the transform.

params.name: zscale
params.desc: The scale factor in the z direction for the transform.

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(20, 30, 0)
scale = 10
transformation = Geom::Transformation.scaling(point, scale)
notes: This has been fixed in SketchUp 2018 but in previous versions it might yield an unexpected transformation. It sets the 16th value to the scaling factor. Something not all extensions reading the ...

methods.name: translation
methods.summary: The .translation method is used to create a transformation that does translation.
methods.example:
vector = Geom::Vector3d.new(0, 1, 0)
transformation = Geom::Transformation.translation(vector)

methods.summary: Instance Methods The #* method is used to do matrix multiplication using the transform.
methods.example:
point1 = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
point2 = Geom::Point3d.new(2, 2, 2)
transformation = Geom::Transformation.new(point1)
# The result is a Point3d(12, 22, 32)
new_point = transformation * point2

methods.name: clone
methods.summary: The #clone method is used to create a copy of a transformation.
methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
transformation = Geom::Transformation.new(point)
new_transformation = transformation.clone

methods.name: identity?
methods.summary: The #identity? method is used to determine if a transformation is the IDENTITY transform.

returns.desc: true if the transformation is the identity

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
transformation = Geom::Transformation.new(point)
# Returns false
status = transformation.identity?
notes: As of SketchUp 2018, this now looks at the data to determine if the transformation is identity. Prior to SU2018, this only looks at the flag to see if the transform has not been modified. If the ...

methods.name: initialize
methods.summary: You can use this method or one of the more specific methods for creating specific kinds of Transformations.

params.name: Creates
params.desc: a Transformation from a 16 element Array.

returns.desc: identity transformation.

methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
transformation = Geom::Transformation.new(point)
notes: Versions prior to SU2018 would produce transformations which didn't always work right in SketchUp. See .scaling for more info.

methods.name: inverse
methods.summary: The #inverse method is used to retrieve the inverse of a transformation.
methods.example:
point = Geom::Point3d.new(10, 20, 30)
transformation = Geom::Transformation.new(point)
new_transformation = transformation.inverse
notes: As of SketchUp 2026, this will raise an error if the Geom::Transformation is not invertible. Prior to 2026 this would silently attempt to invert the transformation possibly returning in an invalid ...
raises: ArgumentError if the Geom::Transformation is not invertible (as of Sketchup 2026)

methods.name: invert!
methods.summary: The #invert! method sets the transformation to its inverse.

vector1 = Geom::Vector2d.new(0, 2)

vector1 = Geom::Vector2d.new(0, 2)

vector1 = Geom::Vector2d.new(1, 0)

vector = Geom::Vector2d.new(1, 2)

The Layout::Document.open method gives you a handle to a Layout::Document, and from there you can use the document-level methods to start getting information and making changes.

If the Layout::Entity is a Layout::Group, then the Layout::Group along with all of its children will be added to the Layout::Document.

methods.name: export
methods.summary: The #export method exports the Layout::Document to a given file format. It knows which format to export based on the file extension you place on the file name. For example, a filename of "thing.pdf" will export a PDF file, whereas "thing.png" will export a set of PNG images. For LayOut version 2020.1, valid extensions include .pdf, .jpg, and .png.

params.name: file_path
params.desc: The file or image set to create. The directory path must already exist. The path must include the file extension.

params.name: options
params.desc: An optional hash of settings for the export.

methods.example:
PDF Export Examples
doc = Layout::Document.open("c:/path/to/document.layout")

# Export pdf file on a PC, with default settings.
doc.export("c:/my_export.pdf")

# Export pages one through three at high quality, compressing jpeg images

# index 1.

# ...

The last page to export.
A string specifying the range of pages to export. The format can include individual page numbers and ranges of pages, separated by commas (e.g., "1,3-5"). This was added in LayOut 2024.0
Whether to compress images in the document. This is valid only for image compression for PDF exports.
The compression quality for JPEG images. This is valid only for the quality of the compression of images for PDF exports.
The resolution in dots per inch for the exported images. This option is only valid for image exports.

# We move the second rectangle to the same group.

Layout::Group.summary: A group is a special type of Layout::Entity that does not belong to a Layout::Layer and contains other Layout::Entitys as children. A Layout::Group's children may include other Layout::Groups, allowing for a hierarchical tree structure of Layout::Entitys. A Layout::Group must contain at least one child and will be automatically collapsed if an operation is performed that results in the Layout::Group being empty.

methods.name: entities
methods.summary: Instance Methods The #entities method returns the Layout::Entities that belong to the Layout::Group.
methods.example:

entities = group.entities

methods.name: initialize
methods.summary: The #initialize method creates a new Layout::Group.
methods.example:
doc = Layout::Document.open("C:/path/to/document.layout")
entities = doc.shared_entities
entities.each { |entity|
  entity_array.push(entity)
}
group = Layout::Group.new(entity_array)
raises: [ArgumentError] if entities is empty.
[ArgumentError] if entities contains Layout::Entitys that belong to different Layout::Documents
[ArgumentError] if entities contains a mix of Layout::Entitys that belong to a Layout::Document and Layout::Entitys that don't belong to a Layout::Document
[ArgumentError] if entities contains Layout::Entitys on both shared and non-shared Layout::Layers, or on non-shared Layout::Layers belonging to different Layout::Pages
[ArgumentError] if entities contains the same Layout::Entity more than once

methods.name: connect
methods.summary: Instance Methods The #connect method connects the Layout::Label to the given Layout::ConnectionPoint. The leader line will be adjusted to point at the Layout::ConnectionPoint. The Layout::Label must be in the same Layout::Document as the Layout::ConnectionPoint. If both the Layout::Label and the Layout::ConnectionPoint's Layout::Entity are on non-shared Layout::Layers, they must be on the same Layout::Page.
methods.example:
text = "A label"
leader_type = Layout::Label::LEADER_LINE_TYPE_BEZIER
target_point = Geom::Point2d.new(1, 1)
bounds = Geom::Bounds2d.new(2, 1, 1, 1)
label = Layout::Label.new(text, leader_type, target_point, bounds)
rect = Layout::Rectangle.new([4, 4, 4, 4])

doc = Layout::Document.new
doc.add_entity(label, doc.layers.first, doc.pages.first)
doc.add_entity(rect, doc.layers.first, doc.pages.first)

point = Geom::Point2d.new(4, 4)
# Create a Connection Point to a LayOut Entity in the Document
cp = Layout::ConnectionPoint.new(rect, point)
label.connect(cp)
raises: [LockedLayerError] if the Layout::Label is on a locked Layout::Layer
[LockedEntityError] if the Layout::Label is locked
[ArgumentError] if the Layout::Label is not in the same Layout::Document as the Layout::ConnectionPoint
[ArgumentError] if both the Layout::Label and the Layout::ConnectionPoint are on non-shared Layout::Layers, but are not on the same Layout::Page.

Layout::Layer.summary: This is the interface to a LayOut Layer Definition. A layer definition specifies the document-wide information about a layer. To access the entities on a layer for a given page, use Layout::LayerInstance.

methods.summary: Instance Methods The #== method checks to see if the two Layout::Layers are equal. This checks whether the Ruby Objects are pointing to the same internal object.

Each Layout::Page has one Layout::LayerInstance for each Layout::Layer in the Layout::Document. ...

methods.name: reorder_entity

params.name: entity
params.desc: The Layout::Entity to reorder

params.name: index
params.desc: The desired index of the Layout::Entity

methods.example:
doc = Layout::Document.open("C:/path/to/document.layout")

Layout::LinearDimension.summary: References a linear dimension entity. A Layout::LinearDimension is composed of the following sub-entities: - two 'extension lines' that connect to the Layout::Entity being dimensioned. - a 'dimension line' connecting the ends of the leaders. This may be represented by one or two Layout::Paths depending on appearance. - an optional 'leader line' that is used for small Layout::LinearDimensions. - a 'dimension text' ...

methods.summary: Instance Methods The #auto_scale= method sets whether the scale for the Layout::LinearDimension is set automatically.

end_point = Geom::Point2d.new(5, 5)

methods.name: connect
methods.summary: The #connect method connects the Layout::LinearDimension to one or two Layout::Entitys using the provided Layout::ConnectionPoints. The Layout::LinearDimension must be in the same Layout::Document as the Layout::Entitys, and on the same Layout::Page if the Layout::Entitys are on non-shared Layout::Layers.
methods.example:
doc = Layout::Document.open("C:/path/to/document.layout")
point_1 = Geom::Point2d.new(5, 7.5)
point_2 = Geom::Point2d.new(8.5, 9)
table = Layout::Rectangle.new([point_1, point_2])
doc.add_entity(table, doc.layers.first, doc.pages.first)
start_point = Layout::ConnectionPoint.new(table, point_1)
end_point = Layout::ConnectionPoint.new(table, point_2)
height = 1.0
dim = Layout::LinearDimension.new(Geom::Point2d.new(1, 1),
  Geom::Point2d.new(5, 5), height)
dim.connect(start_point, end_point)
raises: [LockedLayerError] if the Layout::LinearDimension is on a locked Layout::Layer
[LockedEntityError] if the Layout::LinearDimension is locked

Layout::Page.summary: Class for a single page in a LayOut document.

methods.summary: Instance Methods The #== method checks to see if the two Layout::Pages are equal. This checks whether the Ruby Objects are pointing to the same internal object.
methods.example:
doc = Layout::Document.open("C:/path/to/document.layout")
document = doc.pages.first.document
doc.pages.first == document.pages.first

methods.name: attribute_dictionary
methods.summary: The #attribute_dictionary method returns a copy of the page's attribute dictionary with the given name.

page.set_attribute("jane_doe_doc_maker", "made_by_doc_maker", true)
attributes = page.attribute_dictionary("jane_doe_doc_maker")
# Adding to this Layout::Dictionary does not apply to the page's attribute dictionary, use
# Layout::Page#set_attribute.
attributes.merge!(doc_id: 42)

methods.name: delete_attribute

methods.summary: The #document method returns the Layout::Document that the Layout::Page belongs to.

methods.name: entities
methods.summary: The #entities method returns all Layout::Entitys that are on the Layout::Page. This is the equivalent of iterating over all Layout::LayerInstances and using Layout::LayerInstance.entities.

doc = Layout::Document.open("C:/path/to/document.layout")
first_page = doc.pages.first
entities = first_page.entities

methods.name: get_attribute
methods.summary: The #get_attribute method is used to retrieve the value of an attribute in the page's attribute dictionary. If the third parameter, default_value, is not passed and there is no attribute that matches the given name, it returns nil. If default_value is provided and there is no matching attribute it returns the given value. It does not create an attribute with that name though.

params.name: name
params.desc: The name of an attribute dictionary.

params.name: key
params.desc: An attribute key.

params.name: default_value
params.types: String, Boolean, Integer, Float, Hash, Layout::Dictionary, nil
params.desc: A default value to return if no attribute is found.

returns.types: String, Boolean, Integer, Float, Layout::Dictionary, nil
returns.desc: the retrieved value.

doc = Layout::Document.open("C:/path/to/document.layout")

methods.summary: Instance Methods The #initialize method creates a new normal, lozenge, bulged or rounded Layout::Rectangle, depending on the type passed in. lower_right = Geom::Point2d.new(2, 2)

columns = 4

[LockedEntityError] if the Layout::Table is locked

columns = 4

Length.summary: Because length units are used so often in SketchUp, a special class has been added to make it easier to work with length values. You can use a Length object any place that you would use a Float.

methods.summary: Instance Methods The < method is used to see if one length is less than another length. For example, if l1 = 1.0.inch and l2 = 1.000001.inch then l1 == l2 so l1 < l2 should return false.

params.name: length2
params.desc: A length value.

returns.desc: true if length1 is < length2; false if length1 is not < length2

methods.example:
length1 = 12.to_l
length2 = 11.to_l
if length1 < length2
  puts "length1 is less than length2"
else
  puts "length1 is not less than length2"
end

methods.summary: The <= method is used to see if one length is less than or equal to another length.

params.name: length2
params.desc: A length value.

returns.desc: true if length1 is <= length2; false if length1 is not <= length2

methods.example:
length1 = 11.to_l
length2 = 12.to_l
if length1 <= length2
  puts "length1 is less than or equal length2"
else
  puts "length1 is greater than length2"
end

methods.summary: The <=> method is used to see if one length is less than equal or greater than another length. Because we change == for Length to do a test based on a tolerance, we also need to change <=> to also take tolerance into account.

params.name: length2
params.desc: A length value.

returns.desc: the result of the comparison

methods.example:
length1 = 20.to_l
length2 = 30.to_l
result = length1 <=> length2

methods.summary: The == method is used to see if one length is equal to another length. The equality comparison on Length values uses the default tolerance that SketchUp uses for comparing lengths.

params.name: length2
params.desc: A length value.

returns.desc: true if length1 is == length2; false if length1 is not == length2

methods.example:
length1 = 20.to_l
length2 = 30.to_l
is_equal = length1 == length2

methods.summary: The > method is used to see if one length is greater than another length. For example, if l1 = 1.0.inch and l2 = 1.000001.inch then l1 == l2 so l1 > l2 should return false.

params.name: length2
params.desc: A length value.

returns.desc: true if length1 is > length2; false if length1 is not > length2

methods.example:
length1 = 11.to_l
length2 = 12.to_l
if length1 > length2
  puts "length1 is greater than length2"
else
  puts "length1 is not greater than length2"
end

methods.summary: The >= method is used to see if one length is greater than or equal to another length. For example, if l1 = 1.0.inch and l2 = 1.000001.inch then l1 == l2 so l1 >= l2 should return true. Also L1 <= l2 would return true.

params.name: length2
params.desc: A length value.

returns.desc: true if length1 is >= length2; false if length1 is not >= length2

methods.example:
length1 = 11.to_l
length2 = 12.to_l
if length1 >= length2
  puts "length1 is greater than or equal length2"
else
  puts "length1 is less than length2"
end

methods.name: inspect
methods.summary: The inspect method is used to retrieve an unformatted string for the length, which is the length in inches, regardless of the user's model unit settings. See Length.to_s for a way automatically format your Length to the user's model units.

returns.desc: an unformatted length string

methods.example:
length = 55.to_l
str = length.inspect

methods.name: to_f
methods.summary: The to_f method is used to convert a length to a normal float.

returns.desc: the float length value

methods.example:
length = 45.to_l
f = length.to_f

methods.name: to_s
methods.summary: Format a length as a String using the current units formatting settings for the model. (So if the user's model is set to feet, this method will return a nicely formatted length in feet.)

returns.desc: the float length value

methods.example:
length = 55.to_l
str = length.to_s

Sketchup.summary: The Sketchup module contains a number of important utility methods for use in your Ruby scripts. Many of the classes in the API are implemented beneath this module. You can think of the Sketchup module as the "root" of the application tree. Most ruby calls start from the currently active model, and this is accessed via the Sketchup.active_model method.

methods.name: active_model
methods.summary: Class Methods The active_model method returns the currently active SketchUp model. On the PC, this is the only model that one can have access to via the API, but Macintosh versions of SketchUp can have multiple models open at once, in which case the method will return the model that the user currently has focused.

returns.desc: active model object if successful, false if unsuccessful

methods.example:
model = Sketchup.active_model
if !model
  puts "Failure"
else
  # code acting on the model
end

methods.name: add_observer
methods.summary: The add_observer method is used to add an observer to the current object.

params.name: observer
params.desc: An observer.

returns.desc: true if successful, false if unsuccessful.

methods.example: status = Sketchup.add_observer(observer)

methods.name: app_name
methods.summary: The app_name method is used to retrieve the current application name.

returns.desc: the name of the application, either "SketchUp Pro" or "SketchUp". Note: For versions earlier than SketchUp8 M4 (Mac 8.0.15157 and Windows 8.0.15158) this function will return "Google SketchUp Pro" or "Google SketchUp".

methods.example: name = Sketchup.app_name

methods.name: break_edges=
methods.summary: The break_edges= method can be used to disable or enable the break edges feature. Break edges is the SketchUp 7 feature that automatically splits edges that the user draws which cross over one another.

params.name: enabled
params.desc: If true, break edges will be turned on. If false, it will be deactivated.

returns.desc: true if break edges was turned on.

methods.example: Sketchup.break_edges = false

methods.name: break_edges?
methods.summary: The break_edges? method indicates whether the break edges feature is currently turned on. Break edges is the SketchUp 7 feature that automatically splits edges that the user draws which cross over one another. This feature is always on by default and cannot be disabled by the user via the user interface.
methods.example: is_on = Sketchup.break_edges?

Sketchup::Animation.summary: The Sketchup::Animation interface is implemented to create animations inside SketchUp. At any given time, a single animation can be active on a Sketchup::View. To make your own, build a Ruby class that contains the methods described below:

methods.name: nextFrame
methods.summary: Instance Methods The #nextFrame method is invoked by SketchUp to tell the animation to display its next frame. This method should set up the camera and then call Sketchup::View#show_frame. The #nextFrame method is the only required method of the Sketchup::Animation interface that you must implement.

params.name: view
params.desc: The view for the animation.

returns.desc: continue - true if you want the animation to continue on to the next frame, false if you want the animation to stop after this frame.

methods.example:
def nextFrame(view)
  # Insert your handler code for updating the camera or other entities.
  view.show_frame
  return true
end

methods.name: pause
methods.summary: The #pause method is invoked by SketchUp when the animation is paused. This method is optional (you do not need to implement this method unless you want to perform some specialized function when the animation is paused). You cannot call this method in your code explicitly and expect an animation to pause, only certain SketchUp events cause the method to be called.
methods.example:
def pause
  # Insert handler code for whatever you need to do when it is paused.
end
notes: The user interface for pausing and resuming animations isn't integrated with the Ruby API in the current version, so this method is probably not useful to you.

methods.name: resume
methods.summary: The #resume method is invoked by SketchUp when the animation is resumed after being paused. This method is optional (you do not need to implement this method unless you want to perform some specialized function when the animation is resumed). You cannot call this method in your code explicitly and expect an animation to stop, only certain SketchUp events cause the method to be called.
methods.example:
def resume
  # Insert your handler code for whatever you need to do as you resume.
end
notes: The user interface for pausing and resuming animations isn't integrated with the Ruby API in the current version, so this method is probably not useful to you.

methods.name: stop
methods.summary: The #stop method is invoked by SketchUp when the animation is stopped. This method is optional (you do not need to implement this method unless you want to perform some specialized function when the animation is stopped). You cannot call this method in your code explicitly and expect an animation to stop, only certain SketchUp events cause the method to be called.
methods.example:
class MyAnimation
  def stop
    # Insert your handler code for cleaning up after your animation.
  end
end
notes: Do not call Sketchup::View#animation= from this method. This will cause a recursive loop and crash SketchUp 2017 and earlier versions. As of SketchUp 2018 this will raise a RunTimeError.

  return true
